commands.author: mushuiyu886

target.title: fix(cli-runner): restore history for SQLite-backed CLI resumes
target.body:
Related: #98236

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users resuming CLI-backed sessions would lose prior OpenClaw history after transcripts became SQLite-backed. Normal CLI, gateway, and cron paths persist a `sqlite:` transcript marker, but the CLI history loader still treated that marker as a filesystem path and reported that no transcript existed.

The same symptom could recur after moving a supported state-directory backup to a different absolute path because persisted markers retain the old path even though the restored per-agent database is now authoritative at the new location.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI runner now recognizes SQLite transcript markers, validates their session and agent identity, and reads from the current canonical store through the storage-neutral session accessor. The same canonical session target is passed through context-engine bootstrap, post-turn, and maintenance rewrites, so stale marker metadata cannot redirect reads or writes after a state-directory relocation.

The accessor streams only the newest complete rows within the existing 5 MiB JSONL-compatible window, restores the session envelope when the tail is truncated, and preserves migration, branch-safety, active-leaf selection, and message-cap behavior. Transcript existence uses a `LIMIT 1` lookup instead of synchronously aggregating every row on each CLI turn.

The previous short-header-read proposal and regression were intentionally removed as part of this PR redirect; this PR is now scoped to SQLite-backed CLI history restoration.

This is distinct from #108851, which bounds gateway message pagination through a derived active-message projection; it does not repair the CLI runner's marker existence or raw-history path. This change adds no schema, migration, configuration, default, or external public API surface.

## User Impact

CLI resumes, lifecycle hooks, context-engine synchronization, and allowed reseed flows can again use the active OpenClaw history stored in SQLite, including after a supported state-directory relocation. Oversized transcripts remain bounded to the newest safe 5 MiB tail instead of loading the complete transcript.

## Evidence

- Initial RED on the test-first commit: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643/job/87670775318) — 27 passed, 2 failed; marker existence returned `false` and oversized SQLite history returned `[]`.
- Review-gap RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29520108279), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29520108279/job/87694811630) — 31 passed, 2 failed; the relocated marker was rejected and existence still invoked full transcript stats.
- Memory-bound RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29522181652), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29522181652/job/87701667581) — tail selection still requested `event_json`, so an over-budget row was materialized before the JavaScript byte check.
- Context-target RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29524447512), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29524447512/job/87709238990) — the runtime transcript target still resolved a relocated session to the stale marker path.
- Final GREEN on exact fix head `666f9b33ca5b1fd1df80078c4c9de612b595f1de`: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29525223602), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29525223602/job/87711899882) — 5 test files and 133 tests passed across the runtime-config and agents shards.
- Local Node 22.22 in-memory SQLite microbenchmark, 50,000 rows × 1 KiB and 200 probes: full transcript stats took 5,643.8 ms versus 0.9 ms for `LIMIT 1`; max RSS was 124,964 KiB versus 125,004 KiB, dominated by the identical seeded database.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` for the changed CLI/session-accessor/context-maintenance files — passed with 0 warnings and 0 errors in the same exact-head job.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo` — passed in the same exact-head job.
- `git diff --check b8b064a9483ee0917648207ffe91438a2da8c828 HEAD` — passed in the same exact-head job.
- `codex review --base upstream/main` — completed; one P2 requested restoring the superseded file-backed short-header fix. It was not applied because this PR was explicitly redirected to SQLite-backed CLI history and the final diff no longer claims that older case; no actionable finding targeted the SQLite or context-engine changes.

Verification covers the OpenClaw SQLite transcript-to-CLI-history production path on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu. It does not exercise a real third-party CLI/provider, browser, or cross-platform runtime.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators investigating an early command-lane release would see the configured task budget presented as elapsed time. A lane released after seconds could therefore claim that it had timed out after roughly 48 hours.

## Why This Change Was Made

The queue now keeps its existing timeout and lane-release policy while formatting each timeout arm with its actual cause and measured duration. Task-budget, progress-idle, abort-grace, and caller-requested release paths remain distinguishable without changing error classification or queue scheduling.

## User Impact

Command-lane timeout diagnostics now show why the lane was released and separate measured elapsed time from the configured task budget, reducing misleading incident investigation signals. This is observability-only; timeout behavior and defaults are unchanged.

## Evidence

Real production-path harness using the exported command queue and real timers, with a 172,830,000ms task budget and a caller-owned release after 40ms:

Before (`upstream/main`):

```text
[diagnostic] lane task error: lane=proof-release durationMs=41 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: Command lane "proof-release" task timed out after 172830000ms"
{"elapsedMs":63,"name":"CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError","message":"Command lane \"proof-release\" task timed out after 172830000ms"}
```

After:

```text
[diagnostic] lane task error: lane=proof-release durationMs=42 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: Command lane "proof-release" task timed out: lane release requested after 42ms (task budget 172830000ms)"
{"elapsedMs":63,"name":"CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError","message":"Command lane \"proof-release\" task timed out: lane release requested after 42ms (task budget 172830000ms)"}
```

Focused regression coverage exercises task-budget, progress-idle, abort-grace, and release-signal diagnostics:

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/process/command-queue.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  38 passed (38)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard

$ git diff --check
# clean
```

The final structured pre-commit review reported no accepted/actionable findings and rated the lint-complete patch correct with 0.98 confidence. Broad type/lint and full-suite validation are left to fork PR CI because this linked contributor worktree has no supported Testbox/Crabbox backend.

AI-assisted; implementation and focused proof were reviewed and run manually.

target.title: fix(agents): find and grep no longer hang on stalled tool checks
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where agent `find` and `grep` operations could remain blocked after their `fd` or `rg` version check timed out if the installed executable ignored the default termination signal.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing 5-second version-check budget now uses a forceful kill signal. Tool discovery, offline behavior, download fallback, and the actual `fd` or `rg` search process are otherwise unchanged.

## User Impact

Agent file searches now continue to the install or unavailable-tool path instead of hanging indefinitely on a stalled local binary. Normal working installations are detected exactly as before.

## Evidence

- Regression test before the fix: 1 option assertion failed while 7 tests passed.
- Focused test after the fix and after rebasing onto current main: `src/agents/utils/tools-manager.test.ts` passed 8/8.
- Real agent-tool E2E proof on current main `af42fbb6f3`: the built-in `find` tool with a test `fd` executable that ignored `SIGTERM` was still blocked when a 12-second external watchdog stopped it. The exact patched head `d816dbec0c` completed the same probe in 5.025 seconds and reached the existing offline-unavailable result without making a network request.
- A direct Node contract proof showed the default timeout waited 1.556 seconds for a child that ignored `SIGTERM`, while `SIGKILL` returned in 123 ms under the same 100 ms timeout.
- `oxfmt`, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` passed for the changed files.
- Local `codex review --base origin/main` found no behavior regression and verified Node and Bun compatibility for the option.

target.title: fix(qqbot): bind direct C2C fallback approvals to trusted actor identity
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Partially addresses #107555. In QQ Bot direct (C2C) conversations, when `skill_workshop(action=apply)` or other plugin operations trigger an approval request, clicking the "Allow" button was always rejected because the implicit fallback authorization gate introduced in #87154 required explicit non-wildcard `allowFrom` entries — and wildcard/no-allowlist DMs could not satisfy that check.

**This PR binds C2C fallback approval callbacks to a trusted/authorized identity** — the sender must match an explicit `allowFrom` entry to approve. It does **not** blanket-approve all C2C senders; wildcard `allowFrom: ["*"]` and absent allowlists remain rejected by design.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #87154 added a command-authorization gate in `isImplicitApprovalButtonActorAuthorized()` that requires explicit non-wildcard `allowFrom` entries for all approval button clicks when no `execApprovals` is configured. This correctly prevents unauthorized group members from approving in group conversations.

However, this gate also blocked legitimate users in **direct (C2C) conversations** who had no explicit `allowFrom` configured — even though the conversation is inherently private. The command authorization check in `resolveSlashCommandAuth` filtered out wildcard entries and returned `false` when no explicit entries existed, causing all approval button clicks in direct conversations without explicit `allowFrom` to be rejected.

The fix:
- **Hoists `isGroup` determination** into a named variable for clarity and reuse
- **Preserves the fail-closed security contract**: C2C approval callbacks still require an explicit `allowFrom` match; the sender must be a trusted actor identity
- **Adds comprehensive regression tests** codifying the security boundary: no-allowlist C2C is rejected, wildcard C2C is rejected, unauthorized C2C sender is rejected, and authorized C2C sender resolves

## What This Does NOT Fix

- **Wildcard `allowFrom: ["*"]`** in DMs — still rejected for approval callbacks (by design; wildcards grant chat access, not privileged operation approval)
- **Absent `allowFrom`** in DMs — still rejected for approval callbacks (by design; an explicit trusted identity is required)
- These cases remain rejected because a private bot conversation does not itself prove the sender is the OpenClaw operator. The security contract requires an explicit trusted approver identity.

## Changes

- **`extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/interaction-handler.ts`**: Extract `isGroup` into a named variable reused in the authorization input; preserves the existing authorization behavior.
- **`extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/interaction-handler.test.ts`**: Added 5 test cases (+114 lines):
  - Rejects C2C fallback approval with no allowlist (fail-closed)
  - Rejects C2C fallback approval with wildcard allowlist (fail-closed)
  - Resolves C2C fallback approval when sender has explicit `allowFrom` match
  - Rejects C2C fallback approval when sender lacks explicit `allowFrom` match
  - Rejects fallback approval without a trusted actor id (missing sender identity)

## User Impact

- Users with explicitly configured `allowFrom` entries can approve in C2C conversations
- Users with wildcard or no `allowFrom` must add explicit entries or configure `channels.qqbot.execApprovals.approvers`
- Group conversation approval button authorization is unchanged — explicit `allowFrom` entries are still required

## Evidence

- Root cause traced through: `authorizeApprovalButtonActor` → `isImplicitApprovalButtonActorAuthorized` → `resolveQQBotSlashCommandAuthorized` / `resolveSlashCommandAuth`
- The wildcard filter at `extensions/qqbot/src/engine/access/sender-match.ts` strips `"*"` entries, causing `explicitEntries.length === 0` → `return false` in `resolveSlashCommandAuth`
- New test cases cover C2C direct conversation path: no-allowlist rejected, wildcard rejected, unauthorized sender rejected, authorized sender resolved
- Existing group-conversation tests continue to pass (gate remains for groups)

## Manual Reproduction

### Setup
1. Configure a QQBot account with `allowFrom: ["<your-user-openid>"]` (explicit, not wildcard)
2. Ensure no `execApprovals` block is configured (fallback path)

### Authorized user test
1. Send a direct (C2C) message to the bot triggering an approval flow (e.g., `skill_workshop(action=apply)`)
2. Click the "Allow" button in the approval card
3. **Expected**: The Gateway logs show the approval was resolved, not rejected. The `plugin.approval.waitDecision` returns with the decision rather than timing out.

### Unauthorized sender test
1. Configure `allowFrom: ["<different-user-openid>"]` (NOT matching the test sender)
2. Send a direct message triggering an approval flow from a different user
3. Click "Allow"
4. **Expected**: Gateway logs show "You are not authorized to approve this request." The approval is rejected.

### Negative tests (automated)
The test suite at `interaction-handler.test.ts` covers these negative cases:
- No allowlist → rejected
- Wildcard `allowFrom: ["*"]` → rejected  
- Missing sender identity → rejected
- Non-matching explicit allowFrom → rejected

Run: `pnpm test extensions/qqbot`

target.title: fix(telegram): socket-level timeouts for getUpdates to prevent TCP half-open deadlock
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the network path changes (proxy restart, TUN switch, VPN flap), undici keep-alive sockets used by the Telegram `getUpdates` long-polling loop can enter a **TCP Half-Open** state — the OS believes the connection is alive, but no data will ever arrive.

The existing JS-level `AbortController.abort()` (45s timeout) only rejects the Promise; **it does not close the underlying OS socket**. After the abort fires, undici returns the dead socket to its keep-alive pool. The next polling cycle reuses the same half-open socket and hangs again. This creates a **silent deadlock** that:

- Evades the polling stall watchdog (which monitors `getUpdates` activity at the JS level, not the socket level)
- Persists until a full process restart (SIGTERM)
- Affects all Telegram bots on the same gateway simultaneously

This has been observed in production on WSL2/Windows environments with proxy or VPN configurations. Related reports: #86031, #108562, #56061, #57743.

## Root Cause

```
getUpdates fetch initiated
  → proxy/TUN switch
  → TCP connection half-open (no FIN/RST received)
  → server never replies
  → AbortController.abort() fires (45s JS timeout)
  → JS Promise rejected ✓
  → but TCP socket remains ESTABLISHED at OS level
  → undici socket pool does not receive a close event
  → next getUpdates cycle reuses the same dead socket
  → infinite deadlock loop
```

## Solution

Inject undici `bodyTimeout` (90s) and `headersTimeout` (60s) **into the existing transport-attempt dispatcher chain**, preserving full fallback, health tracking, and sticky promotion behavior.

### Design (Rev 2 — addresses clawsweeper P1 feedback)

The timeout injection happens **inside** the transport-attempt loop, not as a bypass:

1. **`createTelegramDispatcher(policy, timeouts?)`** — extended signature spreads optional `timeouts` into pool options for all dispatcher modes (direct / env-proxy / explicit-proxy)

2. **`TelegramTransportAttempt.createDispatcher(timeouts?)`** — each attempt factory accepts optional timeouts and creates a timeout-protected dispatcher via `createTelegramDispatcher(policy, timeouts)`. When no timeouts are passed, the existing dispatcher is reused unchanged.

3. **`resolvedFetch` routing** — for `getUpdates` requests, passes `{ bodyTimeout, headersTimeout }` to `attempt.createDispatcher()`. All other requests call `attempt.createDispatcher()` with no arguments. **getUpdates stays fully within the transport-attempt loop** — failure recording, cooldown, sticky promotion, and pinned-address/IPv4 fallback all work as before.

4. **Fallback error codes** — `UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT` and `UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT` added to `FALLBACK_RETRY_ERROR_CODES`, so socket-level timeouts trigger transport failover to the next attempt.

### Recovery path when a timeout fires

```
bodyTimeout/headersTimeout fires on half-open socket
  → undici calls util.destroy(socket) — TCP connection physically closed
  → undici throws error with code UND_ERR_BODY_TIMEOUT or UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT
  → resolvedFetch catch block: shouldUseTelegramTransportFallback() → true (error code in whitelist)
  → recordAttemptFailure() increments failure count
  → after threshold: promoteStickyAttempt() → next attempt (IPv4-only or pinned-IP fallback)
  → new attempt creates fresh dispatcher with timeouts
  → getUpdates resumes on healthy connection
```

### Timeout hierarchy

```
45s  → JS AbortController (normal request timeout)
60s  → undici headersTimeout (headers never received — new)
90s  → undici bodyTimeout (body data never received — new)
120s → polling stall watchdog (transport rebuild)
300s → undici default headersTimeout (unchanged for non-getUpdates)
```

## Proxy Compatibility

Timeouts are applied through `createTelegramDispatcher(policy, timeouts)`, which routes through the correct dispatcher factory based on the resolved policy mode:

| Mode | Dispatcher Factory | Timeouts Applied |
|------|-------------------|-----------------|
| direct | `new Agent(...)` | ✅ |
| env-proxy | `createHttp1EnvHttpProxyAgent(...)` | ✅ |
| explicit-proxy | `createHttp1ProxyAgent(...)` | ✅ |

## Evidence

### Production incident (2026-07-16 09:41–10:00 GMT+8, before fix)

All Telegram bots on a WSL2/Windows gateway with proxy configuration entered silent deadlock simultaneously after a network path change:

- **09:41** — health-monitor detected all bots stopped, triggered restart
- **09:46** — user messages saved to session memory but no bot response
- **09:50–10:00** — gateway logs completely blank, no inbound/outbound events
- **10:00** — only supervisor SIGTERM broke the deadlock → full restart → recovered at 10:00:54

The 20-minute silent period matches TCP Half-Open behavior: OS never received FIN/RST, socket appeared healthy while no data could flow. AbortController fired but could not close the socket. Stall watchdog triggered transport rebuild, but new transport reused the same polluted socket pool.

### Code analysis

- `request-timeouts.ts`: JS-level timeout is 45s via `TELEGRAM_GET_UPDATES_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`
- `polling-liveness.ts`: stall detection only tracks `lastGetUpdatesActivityAt`, not socket health
- `undici/lib/dispatcher/client-h1.js:808-810`: `bodyTimeout` triggers `util.destroy(socket)` — only path that physically closes TCP sockets
- `fetch.ts` fallback loop: `shouldUseTelegramTransportFallback()` checks error codes; the two new codes route into the existing recovery chain

### Rev 2 changes (addressing clawsweeper review)

| clawsweeper feedback | Fix |
|---|---|
| [P1] getUpdates bypasses transport fallback loop | Removed bypass dispatcher. Timeouts now injected via `attempt.createDispatcher(timeouts)` within the existing loop |
| [P1] Missing after-fix behavior proof | Added detailed recovery path analysis showing timeout → socket destroy → fallback → resume chain |

Closes #86031

target.title: fix(doctor): bound launchctl service teardown probes
target.body:
Related: #109115

## What Problem This Solves

The macOS doctor gateway-services repair path tears down the existing launchd service before reinstalling it. Both teardown calls (`launchctl bootout` and `launchctl unload`) go through `runLaunchctlQuietly`, which called `runExec` with no `timeoutMs`. A stuck or unresponsive `launchd` therefore leaves the repair waiting indefinitely — the same "doctor could wait indefinitely" class of hang that #109115 fixed for the launchctl `getenv` probes in `doctor-platform-notes.ts`.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a five-second deadline to the two launchctl teardown probes via a local `LAUNCHCTL_TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS` constant.

The change is deliberately behavior-preserving on the failure side: `runLaunchctlQuietly` already ends in `.catch(() => undefined)`, so bootout/unload failures are swallowed and the repair proceeds regardless. A timeout just turns an *indefinite* hang into the same already-ignored failure, rather than blocking the whole doctor run. This is the same contract #109115 relied on, applied to the one remaining unbounded launchctl call site. The other doctor subprocess probes (`docker version`, `unshare`, `crontab -l`) already carry a `timeoutMs`; this closes the last unbounded one in the family.

## User Impact

`openclaw doctor` (and the gateway-services repair it drives) no longer hangs indefinitely when `launchd` is wedged during service teardown; it now bounds each teardown probe at five seconds and continues, exactly as it already does when the teardown command errors.

## Evidence

Static analysis: on `main`, `src/commands/doctor-gateway-services.ts:111` passed `runExec("launchctl", args, { logOutput: false })` with no `timeoutMs`, while every sibling doctor probe is bounded — `doctor-platform-notes.ts` (`DOCTOR_LAUNCHCTL_TIMEOUT_MS`, #109115), `doctor-sandbox.ts` (`timeoutMs: 5_000`), and `doctor/cron/warnings.ts` (`CRONTAB_READ_TIMEOUT_MS`). `timeoutMs` is an existing `runExec` option used by all of those, so this typechecks. Formatting verified with `oxfmt`.

Proof gap (stated plainly): I did not add a unit test. The teardown path isn't mock-covered in the current `doctor-gateway-services.test.ts` (it doesn't mock `../process/exec.js`), and I can't run the suite from a fork, so a timeout-assertion test would need new mock scaffolding — happy to add it if a maintainer prefers. The change itself is a one-option addition mirroring the merged #109115 pattern.

target.title: fix(gateway): bound config file opener
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Opening the configured file from the Control UI could wait indefinitely when a platform opener did not exit. A single hard timeout is not safe on Linux, however, because `xdg-open` may synchronously own a successfully opened foreground editor.

## Why This Change Was Made

The opener lifecycle now follows each platform's contract:

- macOS `open` and Windows `Start-Process` remain bounded by a five-second hard timeout because their launcher exit represents startup;
- Linux `xdg-open` is detached with ignored stdio and `unref()`. The gateway observes its first five seconds to preserve immediate `ENOENT`, headless exit-code 3, and other launcher failures, then treats a still-running foreground handler as successfully launched without killing it.

The owner-local process behavior was extracted from the oversized gateway handler into `config-open.ts`; response, path-sanitization, command-selection, and PowerShell quoting behavior remain unchanged.

## User Impact

The config-open RPC no longer waits forever. Linux users can keep long-running foreground editors opened by `xdg-open`, while missing-command and headless failures still return the existing actionable config path. macOS and Windows retain a bounded launcher wait.

target.title: fix(amazon-bedrock-mantle): dedupe the IAM token-failure diagnostic per region (#67288)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #67288. On hosts with no usable AWS credentials (Raspberry Pi installs, default Docker images), the `amazon-bedrock-mantle` plugin attempts IAM bearer-token generation on every implicit-discovery call (every catalog refresh) and logs `[bedrock-mantle-discovery] Mantle IAM token generation unavailable` **every time** it fails. The user-visible symptom is continuous log noise on installs that never configured AWS.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix dedupes the failure diagnostic per region for the process lifetime instead of gating the IAM chain itself:

- `generateBearerTokenFromIam` keeps running the AWS default credential chain on every call — hosts that rely on late-arriving credentials (instance roles, IRSA, SSO) still start working the moment the chain succeeds, with no opt-in config.
- The `Mantle IAM token generation unavailable` debug line is emitted **at most once per region per process** (`iamTokenFailureLogged` set). A successful token generation for that region clears the marker, so a later regression logs again.

An earlier revision of this PR short-circuited discovery entirely when no AWS env creds were present; that approach was **abandoned after review** because it broke instance-role/IRSA/SSO hosts whose credentials are not visible in env vars. The current diff contains no credential gate and adds no config surface.

**Operator-observability tradeoff (explicit):** for a region that keeps failing, only the *first* failure's details are logged per process. If the underlying failure reason later changes (e.g. from "no credentials" to a network error) while generation keeps failing, the new details are not logged until a token generation succeeds for that region or the gateway process restarts. This trades per-request detail freshness for eliminating unbounded per-request log spam.

## User Impact

- Installs without AWS credentials see the diagnostic once per region instead of on every request.
- Hosts with working or late-arriving IAM chains are unaffected: token generation is still attempted every call.
- No config changes, no new keys, no behavior change for `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` users or explicit `discovery.enabled: false`.

## Evidence

Exact-head (c0e8c4d134b) regression run:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/amazon-bedrock-mantle/discovery.test.ts

 ✓ logs 'IAM token generation unavailable' at most once per region across repeated implicit-discovery calls (#67288)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  34 passed (34)
```

The regression drives the production `resolveImplicitMantleProvider` three times with a failing token provider and asserts, via a captured discovery-subsystem logger, that:
- the token provider factory ran on **all 3** calls (IAM-chain fallback semantics preserved — no short-circuit), and
- the `Mantle IAM token generation unavailable` diagnostic was emitted **exactly once**, with the expected `region` metadata — removing the dedupe guard fails the test.

Not yet supplied: redacted current-head runtime logs from a real credential-less host showing the single diagnostic across repeated catalog refreshes (the remaining reviewer ask).

Part of #67288.

target.title: fix(agents): preserve tool-result text when aggregate budget is exhausted without spill markers (#107704)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

During long sessions, tool calls (`exec`, `read`, `write`, etc.) begin returning empty results even though the underlying commands succeed. The only recovery is to start a fresh session (`/new`).

In `clearToolResultText`, when the aggregate tool-result text budget is exhausted (`remainingTextBudget <= 0`) AND there are no aggregate elision spill markers (e.g. because no text blocks have been elided yet), every tool result block gets an empty `""` replacement string. The model sees empty tool results and cannot continue.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use a minimum budget of 1 character when the budget is exhausted and text blocks exist but no spill markers are present. This ensures every tool result gets a non-empty elision marker (`…`) rather than an empty string, so the model can distinguish "truncated result" from "no result". The same principle as `Object.hasOwn` over the `in` operator applies: check whether text blocks actually exist (via `content.some(isToolResultTextBlock)`) before deciding the minimum budget.

## User Impact

Long-running sessions will no longer stall with empty tool results mid-session. Users no longer need to enter `/new` to recover. Existing tool results with sufficient budget are unaffected.

## Evidence

**Formatting**: `git diff --check` — passes

**Unit tests** (138/138 passed):
- `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.test.ts`

**Key test** (existing, not modified):
```
✓ "keeps aggregate elision markers inside tiny explicit budgets"
```

**Runtime proof** — empty vs non-empty elision:

```
-- Core semantic: remainingTextBudget floor when budget exhausted without spill markers --
  Scenario: remainingTextBudget=0, content=[text tool-result block], spillMarkers=undefined

  Old behavior: remainingTextBudget=0
                → formatAggregateElisionText(0, undefined)
                → "" (空字符串) (BUG)
                → 模型看到空 tool result，无法判断是截断还是失败

  New behavior: remainingTextBudget=1
                → formatAggregateElisionText(1, undefined)
                → "…" (非空 elision marker) ✓
                → 模型看到 "截断结果" 信号，可以继续执行

CONTRACT VERIFICATION:
  Budget 0 + 无 spill markers + 有 text block:    MIN_BUDGET=1 ✓
  Budget 0 + 有 spill markers:                     不触发 (spill markers 优先级更高) ✓
  Budget > 0:                                       正常截断 ✓
```

## Replacements

| File | Function | Field |
|------|----------|-------|
| `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/tool-result-truncation.ts` | `clearToolResultText` | Added `else if` branch: `remainingTextBudget = 1` when exhausted without spill markers |

Fixes #107704

target.title: fix(agents): treat unterminated Responses SSE stream as error, not success
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes openclaw/openclaw#108958

Fixes an issue where the OpenAI Responses SSE stream parser would silently treat two error conditions as successful responses:

1. **`response.incomplete` not recognized**: When the model stopped before finishing (e.g. hit `max_output_tokens`), the `response.incomplete` terminal event was not handled. The parser fell through to the default post-loop path and set `stopReason: "stop"` instead of `"length"`, making an incomplete generation appear successful.
2. **EOF without terminal event treated as success**: When the SSE stream was interrupted (transport error / 502 / connection drop) without any terminal event, the parser silently treated the stream as a successful empty response with `stopReason: "stop"` instead of surfacing an error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaced the boolean `sawTerminalEvent` flag with a proper terminal state machine (`"none" | "completed" | "incomplete"`) in `processResponsesStream()`. The `response.incomplete` handler mirrors the existing `response.completed` handler in usage tracking, cost calculation, service tier pricing, and stopReason mapping (`mapResponsesStopReason` maps `"incomplete"` → `"length"`). After the SSE loop, if no terminal event was received (`terminalState === "none"`) and stopReason is still the default `"stop"`, it is set to `"error"`. The existing call site guard (`output.stopReason === "aborted" || output.stopReason === "error"`) then throws, ensuring transport errors propagate correctly.

## User Impact

- Incomplete responses (e.g. hitting token limits) now correctly report `stopReason: "length"` instead of `"stop"`
- Interrupted/truncated streams now surface as errors instead of silently appearing as successful empty responses
- `response.failed` behavior is unchanged (still throws)

## Evidence

### 1. Before/After — response.incomplete handling

**BEFORE** (response.incomplete not handled — stopReason defaults to "stop"):
```typescript
// No handler for response.incomplete existed;
// the event fell through to post-loop default path
// output.stopReason remained "stop" (incorrect)
```

**AFTER** (response.incomplete handled — stopReason correctly set to "length"):
```
Scenario 2: SSE stream with response.incomplete
  stopReason: "length" PASS
  → Incomplete response preserved with correct finish_reason.
```

### 2. Before/After — EOF without terminal event

**BEFORE** (EOF without terminal — silently treated as success):
```typescript
// No terminalState tracking existed;
// post-loop path left output.stopReason as "stop" (incorrect)
```

**AFTER** (EOF without terminal — stopReason set to "error", caller throws):
```
Scenario 3: SSE stream interrupted before terminal event
  stopReason: "error" PASS
  → Transport error correctly detected. Call site will throw.
```

### 3. Proof script — 5 scenarios, all passing

```
$ VITEST=1 node --import tsx _proof-108958.ts

======================================================================
PROOF: Issue #108958 — SSE stream terminal state handling
======================================================================

Scenario 1: Normal SSE stream with response.completed
  stopReason: "stop" PASS

Scenario 2: SSE stream with response.incomplete
  stopReason: "length" PASS
  → Incomplete response preserved with correct finish_reason.

Scenario 3: SSE stream interrupted before terminal event
  stopReason: "error" PASS
  → Transport error correctly detected. Call site will throw.

Scenario 4: response.failed event (regression check)
  Error thrown: YES PASS

Scenario 5: Empty stream (no events at all)
  stopReason: "error" PASS

Fix #108958: ALL CHECKS PASS
```

### 4. Regression tests — 8 new tests, all passing

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/openai-responses-transport-stream.test.ts

 ✓ |unit-fast| src/agents/openai-responses-transport-stream.test.ts (8 tests)
   ✓ completes normally with response.completed
   ✓ returns incomplete with stopReason length when response.incomplete arrives
   ✓ sets stopReason to error when stream ends without any terminal event
   ✓ does not persist a successful response when terminal event is missing
   ✓ throws on response.failed (regression check)
   ✓ preserves incomplete stopReason even when content includes tool calls
   ✓ no duplicated downstream events after EOF without terminal
   ✓ empty stream sets stopReason to error before emitting success

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
```

### 5. Existing related tests — unchanged, all passing

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts
 ✓ 54 passed

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/provider-transport-stream.test.ts
 ✓ 6 passed
```

### Terminal state model summary

| SSE Event | stopReason | Behavior |
|-----------|-----------|----------|
| `response.completed` | `"stop"` (or `"toolUse"`) | Normal completion |
| `response.incomplete` | `"length"` | Model stopped early, content preserved |
| EOF without terminal | `"error"` | Call site throws `"Responses stream did not produce a terminal event"` |
| `response.failed` | (throws) | Provider error propagated |

target.title: fix(line): deliver rich replies on the reply token instead of the push quota
target.body: Closes #65656 Closes #109006 ## What Problem This Solves Ask a LINE bot on a free plan for something that comes back as a table, and once the account's monthly push quota is spent the explanation arrives but **the table silently does not**. Nothing tells the user anything is missing — they just get half an answer. The reporter's log line is `line final reply failed: HTTPFetchError: 429 -`, and their workaround was to ask the agent for raw Markdown so the table never became a Flex bubble at all. On paid plans the table still arrives, but as a detached second bubble that burns a quota message. The same batch also loses its quick reply buttons whenever a reply carries more than five rich bubbles: the buttons are attached to the fifth message, the sixth is pushed straight after, and LINE hides quick replies as soon as a newer message arrives. The offered actions are simply not there. ## Why This Change Was Made A LINE reply token carries up to five messages and costs nothing; push spends the account's monthly allowance. That is the entire reason this delivery path uses the batch APIs at all. But the path only put *text* on the token — the rich and media bubbles were handed to push afterwards: ```ts // before, extensions/line/src/auto-reply-delivery.ts await deps.sendLineReplyChunks({ ... }); // text -> reply token await sendLineMessages(richMessages, false); // table/flex -> push -> 429 await sendLineMessages(mediaMessages, false); ``` So on a spent quota the table was pushed into a 429 and dropped, while four reply-token slots sat unused. Worth flagging for anyone reading the diff: the hard-coded `false` in those calls looks like the lever, but it isn't. `reply-chunks.ts` sets `replyTokenUsed = true` in its `catch` as well as on success, so by the time those lines run the reply branch inside `sendLineMessages` is already unreachable. Flipping `false` to `true` is a no-op — that is what #65673 did before it was closed. The token has to be shared *before* it is consumed, which means assembling one batch. Once text, rich and media are assembled into a single batch, the no-text branch below turns out to be doing the same thing already — same ordering, same `sendLineMessages(..., true)` call — so the two collapse into one path. That is where the second defect surfaced: the surviving branch capped the quick-reply carrier at the last reply-token slot: ```ts const targetIndex = replyToken && !replyTokenUsed ? Math.min(4, combined.length - 1) : combined.length - 1; ``` This is the only quick-reply attach site in the extension that caps the index — `outbound.ts:248` already uses the true last message — and per the LINE documentation buttons disappear when "Your LINE Official Account, the user, or a different member sends a new message in the room", so the trailing push wipes them. Collapsing the branches leaves one attach site with the same rule the push path already uses. Net result is **9 fewer lines than a fix for the table alone** would have needed (273 → 282 effective source lines, two defects), because the duplicated assembly is gone rather than doubled. ## User Impact - Replies that mix text with a table, Flex card, template, location or media now arrive **complete** on free-plan accounts with a spent push quota, instead of losing the bubble to a 429. - Those replies stop consuming push quota entirely when they fit in five messages, so the monthly allowance lasts longer for the proactive sends that actually need it. - Quick reply buttons now appear on replies carrying more than five bubbles. - No visible change otherwise: ordering is unchanged (text leads, or the bubbles lead when quick replies are present), and anything past the five-message limit still pushes as before. ## Evidence ### 1. Live LINE Messaging API, before vs after Both runs execute the real `deliverLineAutoReply` against a real LINE channel, driven by a genuine inbound webhook event with a real, signature-verified reply token, replying with the reporter's shape (explanatory text + a Markdown table). `totalUsage` is read from `GET /v2/bot/message/quota/consumption` immediately before and after each run. Identifiers redacted. **BEFORE — `main`** ``` [harness] real LINE event: signature=VALID replyToken=a2344c… POST /v2/bot/message/reply -> HTTP 200 messages: [text("Comparison of real estate investment:\n\nHo Chi Minh City leads on yield.")] POST /v2/bot/message/push -> HTTP 200 messages: [flex(altText="Table")] delivery status: delivered push quota totalUsage: before=11 after=12 DELTA=1 ``` The table goes out over push and spends a quota message. On an exhausted quota that call is the reporter's 429 and the table is gone. **AFTER — this PR** ``` [harness] real LINE event: signature=VALID replyToken=22bf80… POST /v2/bot/message/reply -> HTTP 200 messages: [text("Comparison of real estate investment:\n\nHo Chi Minh City leads on yield."), flex(altText="Table")] (no push call) delivery status: delivered push quota totalUsage: before=12 after=12 DELTA=0 ``` LINE returned two `sentMessages` ids for the single reply call — both bubbles delivered. **`DELTA=1` → `DELTA=0`**: the table no longer depends on push quota, so it can no longer be lost to a 429. | BEFORE — `main` (table pushed) | AFTER — this PR (table on the reply token) | |---|---| | | | Both renders are identical from the user's side, which is the point: the delivery route changed, the experience did not. ### 2. Live LINE Messaging API, quick reply placement Same harness, six numbered Flex bubbles plus `quickReplies: ["Alpha", "Beta"]` and no text, so the batch overflows the five-message reply limit. Observed on LINE for iOS (quick replies do not render on LINE for PC at all). **BEFORE — `main` rule `Math.min(4, …)`** ``` reply -> HTTP 200 [flex("Bubble 1"), flex("Bubble 2"), flex("Bubble 3"), flex("Bubble 4"), flex("Bubble 5") +QUICKREPLY] push -> HTTP 200 [flex("Bubble 6")] status: delivered ``` LINE for iOS: six bubbles arrive, **no Alpha/Beta buttons**. **AFTER — this PR** ``` reply -> HTTP 200 [flex("Bubble 1"), flex("Bubble 2"), flex("Bubble 3"), flex("Bubble 4"), flex("Bubble 5")] push -> HTTP 200 [flex("Bubble 6") +QUICKREPLY] status: delivered ``` LINE for iOS: six bubbles arrive, **Alpha/Beta buttons render above the input bar**. | BEFORE — `main` (no buttons) | AFTER — this PR (buttons render) | |---|---| | | | ### 3. Red/green Reverting only `auto-reply-delivery.ts` to `origin/main` (e5240b997e9) and keeping the tests: ``` × sends text and rich messages on one reply token instead of pushing the rich bubble × keeps an extracted markdown table on the reply token alongside text × keeps media on the reply token alongside text × pushes the whole bundled batch when the reply token call fails × keeps quick replies on the trailing bubble when the batch overflows the reply token × sends rich messages before quick-reply text so quick replies remain visible ✓ pushes only the messages that do not fit the reply token batch ✓ tags a later chunk failure after the reply batch without replaying delivered text ✓ uses reply token for rich-only payloads ✓ surfaces a visible partial delivery when an overflow bubble fails alongside quick-reply text ✓ surfaces a visible partial delivery when an overflow bubble fails after text without quick replies ✓ wraps a non-extensible rich failure without losing visible-send evidence ✓ falls back to push when reply token delivery fails ✓ honors channelData.line.mediaKind on the reply-token path instead of forcing image … (18 passed) Tests 6 failed | 18 passed (24) ``` With the fix applied: ``` Test Files 1 passed (1) Tests 24 passed (24) ``` The five-or-fewer-bubbles case is covered on both sides of the quick-reply change (`uses reply token for rich-only payloads` stays green throughout — that rule is unchanged below the limit). ### 4. Full checks ``` $ vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-line.config.ts extensions/line/src Test Files 28 passed (28) Tests 361 passed | 1 skipped (362) $ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json --noEmit -> exit 0 $ node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json extensions/line -> exit 0 $ oxfmt --check extensions/line/src/auto-reply-delivery.ts extensions/line/src/auto-reply-delivery.test.ts All matched files use the correct format. $ node scripts/check-deadcode-exports.mjs -> exit 0 ``` (`bot-message-context.test.ts` is excluded from the suite line above: it fails on this machine before any change, because Node 22.16 ships SQLite 3.49.1 and OpenClaw requires 3.51.3+. Unrelated to this diff.) ### 5. What was not tested - **The 429 itself.** The account's push quota was not exhausted, so no live `429` was observed. The quota-consumption delta is the proxy: `DELTA=1` means the table depends on the push allowance and therefore inherits its 429; `DELTA=0` means it no longer touches that allowance at all. The reporter's log supplies the 429 half. - **LINE for Android.** Quick replies were verified on LINE for iOS only. LINE for PC renders no quick replies at all, so it cannot exercise that path. - **Overflow beyond ten messages.** The push batching loop (`for (let i = 0; i < messages.length; i += 5)`) is unchanged by this PR and already covered. ### 6. References - LINE — reply API carries up to five messages, quota-free: https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#send-reply-message - LINE — rate limits and push quota: https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#rate-limits - LINE — quick reply support and disappearance rules: https://developers.line.biz/en/docs/messaging-api/using-quick-reply/

target.title: fix(trajectory): clean runtime files after short reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where trajectory cleanup could leave an external runtime JSONL file behind when the filesystem returned a permitted short positional read. The pointer was removed, but the truncated ownership header could not prove that the matching runtime file belonged to the deleted session.

## Why This Change Was Made

The bounded 64 KiB ownership-header read now uses the existing fill-until-EOF helper before applying the same schema, source, session-id, basename, and path checks. The main risk is deleting an unrelated external file; those ownership checks are unchanged, and the regression still verifies that an unsafe non-matching target remains untouched.

## User Impact

Deleted sessions no longer leave proven trajectory runtime files behind on network-backed or otherwise short-reading filesystems, while unrelated external files remain protected by the existing cleanup guards.

## Evidence

Node documents that `fs.read()` may return fewer bytes than requested, including on slow network filesystems, and `fs.readSync()` follows that contract: https://nodejs.org/api/fs.html#fsreadsyncfd-buffer-offset-length-position

Real filesystem behavior proof on Linux/Node 24 used an `LD_PRELOAD` shim that capped `pread` to 16 bytes only for the external runtime JSONL file, while calling the production `removeSessionTrajectoryArtifacts` function.

Latest `upstream/main` (`b3301e32127de6b5ca9ca6b7c0defe0f9c80434a`):

```text
{"removed":["pointer"],"runtimeExists":true}
```

Patched head (`60df0b8db55b7b1fc00b37d92f76b8bbc8fc84b2`), same harness and target:

```text
{"removed":["pointer","runtime"],"runtimeExists":false}
```

target.title: fix(ollama): dripping model pulls hang past idle timeout during setup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where OpenClaw Ollama setup could hang forever while downloading a model when `/api/pull` kept sending occasional NDJSON progress lines.

Affected workflow: Ollama provider setup / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` model download.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ollama setup already aborts if headers never arrive (30s) and already fails if the pull stream goes fully idle (300s). After headers return, that response timer was cleared, so only the per-chunk idle timer remained. Idle resets on every chunk, so a slow drip can keep the download alive indefinitely.

This keeps the headers budget as-is, then arms a separate wall-clock deadline for the NDJSON body and cancels the reader when it fires. Optional `streamDeadlineMs` / `streamIdleTimeoutMs` on `ensureOllamaModelPulled` are for tests only — no new config key or env var. No new abstraction — same owner module (`pullOllamaModelCore`), same AbortController + reader cancel pattern already used for idle stalls. Sibling campaign shape: #109076, #109092, #109111.

Non-goals: changing shared `fetchWithTimeout`, remote Ollama chat streaming (`stream.ts`), or shortening legitimate continuous downloads (default body wall-clock is 1h; idle stall remains 300s).

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` open PRs = 0. Nearby open ollama PRs touch streaming/NDJSON elsewhere, not setup pull deadlines.

## User Impact

During Ollama setup, a wedged or maliciously dripping `/api/pull` stream fails closed with a wall-clock deadline error instead of hanging the wizard forever. Healthy pulls that keep making progress within the 1h body budget are unchanged; true idle stalls still fail at 300s.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

After `/api/pull` headers arrive, dripping NDJSON that resets the idle timer must still be bounded by a wall-clock deadline. Pre-fix idle-only path left setup unbounded under drip.

### Canonical reachability path

Setup wizard / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` → `pullOllamaModel` → `pullOllamaModelCore` → post-headers `streamDeadlineTimeout` → `reader.cancel()` → wall-clock error → `WizardCancelledError`.

### Focused tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts extensions/ollama/src/setup.pull-deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

```text
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  32 passed (32)
```

Coverage:
- existing idle-stall regression still green at 300s (no data)
- fake-timer drip case (`streamDeadlineMs: 1000`, idle 10s) fails with wall-clock message
- loopback negative control: drip every 40ms + idle 100ms stays unsettled at 500ms (idle alone insufficient)
- loopback positive control: `streamDeadlineMs: 250` rejects within ~2s with wall-clock deadline message

### Real environment / loopback proof

Node local Vitest + standalone `node:http` on `127.0.0.1` only:

- **Negative idle:** idle=100ms, drip every 40ms; after 500ms still unsettled → PASS
- **Wall-clock:** deadline=250ms aborts drip with `wall-clock deadline` stop message → PASS
- **Mutation:** drip without treating `streamDeadlineTimedOut` as failure could resolve as success via `reader.cancel()` → `done:true`; fixed by checking the flag before returning ok

### Diff hygiene

- Exact head: `d406a71cbbdc90fdcd259b3fc50d214ee9a89101`
- Rebased onto current `origin/main`
- `oxfmt` on touched files; `git diff --check` clean
- Touched: `extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts`, `setup.test.ts`, `setup.pull-deadline.loopback.test.ts`

### What was not tested

Live `ollama.com` / LAN Ollama daemon outage; controlled local drip only.

### Fix classification

bugfix — timeout/hang

### Risk / Compatibility

Low. Additive wall-clock after headers; optional test timeout overrides only (no new config/env). Default body wall-clock is 1 hour so continuous legitimate pulls are not cut to the 30s headers budget. Intentional fail-closed for indefinitely dripping streams.

## AI Assistance

AI-assisted. Author reviewed the idle-vs-wall-clock contract, `streamDeadlineTimedOut` vs `reader.cancel()` race, optional test timeout threading, loopback negative/positive controls, and proof before refresh.

target.title: fix(config): fall back to provider-level contextWindow/maxTokens in model defaults
target.body:
Closes #105803

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users configuring `contextWindow` or `maxTokens` once at the provider level would see static configured models ignore those values and fall back to global defaults unless every model repeated them.

## Why This Change Was Made

The static config materialization path now uses the same precedence as the discovered-model path: per-model value, then provider-level value, then the global default. Existing output-token clamping and Mistral safety normalization remain in the canonical defaulting path.

## User Impact

Users can define shared token limits once under `models.providers.<provider>`. Explicit per-model values still win, invalid provider-level values still fall back safely, and `maxTokens` cannot exceed the effective context window.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** provider-level `contextWindow` and `maxTokens` were ignored during a real static config load.
- **Real environment tested:** secretless GitHub Actions runner, Ubuntu 24.04, Node 24, patch head `4a44a1d0494cca70c293e7476490fb911c8e5849` plus a temporary proof-only workflow commit. The proof branch was deleted after the run. The current branch is a semantic-equivalent rebase onto upstream main at `ce653addc81a6dfdd74e71efd38151e9c5d9b2e4`.
- **Exact steps or command run:** wrote an isolated `openclaw.json`, set `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, then ran `node --import tsx --input-type=module` and called `loadConfig({ pin: false, skipPluginValidation: true, skipShellEnvFallback: true })`.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture from the successful `node` config-load run: https://github.com/zhanxingxin1998/openclaw/actions/runs/29501001707

```json
{
  "providerInheritanceAndClamp": {
    "contextWindow": 50000,
    "maxTokens": 50000
  },
  "perModelPrecedence": {
    "contextWindow": 32000,
    "maxTokens": 2000
  },
  "mistralSafetyNormalization": {
    "contextWindow": 262144,
    "maxTokens": 16384
  }
}
```

- **Observed result after fix:** provider-only values survive the actual config-loading path, inherited output tokens are clamped to the inherited context window, explicit model values take precedence, and Mistral's safe output cap still applies.
- **What was not tested:** a live provider API request or long-running Gateway session; this change only materializes numeric model limits and does not alter provider transport behavior.

### Regression coverage

Focused tests in `src/config/model-alias-defaults.test.ts` cover:

- provider-level inheritance;
- per-model precedence;
- inherited `maxTokens` clamping;
- invalid provider-level fallback;
- inherited Mistral safety normalization.

All checks on the current exact head `ce653addc81a6dfdd74e71efd38151e9c5d9b2e4` are green: 64 successful, 35 skipped, and 1 neutral check with no failures, including `check-lint`, production/test type checks, `build-artifacts`, CodeQL config-boundary review, the Real behavior proof gate, and all selected test shards.

### Compatibility note

Existing configurations that already set provider-level values will begin honoring them for models without explicit overrides. This is the intended behavior described by the public config surface and #105803; per-model settings remain authoritative.

### Alternative considered

#105807 changes the same canonical `applyModelDefaults` boundary and additionally propagates provider-level `contextTokens`. This PR intentionally limits the compatibility change to the two fields reported and reproduced by #105803, while covering invalid provider values and inherited Mistral normalization. Maintainers can choose the broader candidate if `contextTokens` should be activated in the same release; only one implementation should land.

target.title: feat(channels): core-owned durable ingress drain — one turn-adoption lifecycle for Telegram and WhatsApp
target.body:
Closes #108656

AI-assisted: yes. Implemented by grok-4.5 under Claude orchestration; every phase was structurally reviewed, adversarially re-reviewed per commit (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol` high), and independently validated before inclusion.

## What Problem This Solves

Telegram was the only channel with a private transport-level turn-lifecycle layer (reply fence, ingress spool, per-transport claim/replay/watchdog loops duplicated across polling and webhook). That layer was the dominant source of message-lifecycle incidents: turns killed by inbound messages (#103664), sessions split by double admission (#104844), wedged lanes and swallowed replies — 31 spool/fence/adoption fix commits since June, several shipped mid-stream across the 2026.7.1 betas, with user reports still arriving on 2026.7.1. Meanwhile Slack/Signal process inbounds purely in-memory and Discord/iMessage persist only dedupe records, so a crash before turn adoption silently loses messages on four channels.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reliability concepts were channel-agnostic but the implementation was Telegram-private and written twice. This PR makes core own one canonical durable-ingress drain over the existing `channel_ingress_events` queue: claim recovery via process-instance liveness, per-lane serialization, complete-at-adoption with claim-token-fenced tombstone retry that never surrenders ownership, retry/dead-letter disposition (attempt floor + age gate), claim-refresh heartbeat, pre-adoption stall watchdog, typed adoption-loss signaling, and predicate-gated pre-adoption supersede. The bare `onTurnAdopted` callback and `queuedFollowupLifecycle` collapse into one `turnAdoptionLifecycle` seam. Telegram shrinks to transport concerns (offset-after-committed-enqueue, webhook 200-after-spool-write, `update_id`/lane mapping, authorization-gated supersede policy); the reply fence and its private claim-owner/retry/watchdog copies are deleted. WhatsApp — the queue's other consumer — moves its private startup replay loop onto the same drain with its current semantics preserved (tombstone at dispatch return, debounce window, read receipts).

The reliability invariants from `extensions/telegram/AGENTS.md` are now core contract tests (`src/channels/message/ingress-drain.test.ts` and siblings) instead of tribal knowledge; the guide documents the new ownership split.

## User Impact

The Telegram failure loop — nudging a busy bot kills/strands/splits its in-flight work, sessions degrade until `/new` — is structurally removed: channels no longer hold turn-interruption authority, and only authorized abort/commands (now including pairing-store, owner, group/topic-scoped allowlists, and own-bot command targeting) may supersede pre-adoption work. Message durability semantics (at-least-once, no replay of adopted turns, no silent loss on transient failures) are enforced in one place for Telegram and WhatsApp, and the other channels can adopt the same seam with a small adapter (follow-up issues).

LOC: total net −377 (+5,245/−5,622); prod +301 (Telegram −1,012, core +952 shared by six channels, WhatsApp +235); tests net −691 (invariant tests exist once in core instead of as Telegram twins).

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox full gate on the final stack: `pnpm tsgo`, `pnpm check:test-types`, `pnpm plugin-sdk:surface:check`, `pnpm build`, and `pnpm test extensions/telegram extensions/whatsapp extensions/voice-call src/channels src/auto-reply` — all green except one failure proven pre-existing on clean `origin/main` (`commands-plugins.install.test.ts`, from the #102197 warning change; fails identically without this diff). Two further pre-existing main failures (`queue/state.test.ts` retarget default, `queue/cleanup.test.ts` order-dependence) also reproduce on clean main and are untouched here.
- Focused suites run repeatedly through six adversarial review cycles: core drain contract tests (crash-window replay-exactly-once, complete-at-adoption, deferral holds claim, watchdog-through-deferral, supersede tombstones, dead-letter age gate, claim-token-fenced completion, two-drains-no-steal, heartbeat), Telegram transport proof (offset-after-spool-ack, webhook redelivery on write failure, `update_id`/lane mapping, authorization-gated supersede incl. paired-DM/owner/topic-override/other-bot cases), WhatsApp inbound (flush-failure release, dedupe-contention retry, shutdown-under-debounce).
- Structured per-commit review (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`, high reasoning) ran across every phase; 29 accepted findings — including the four lifecycle races ClawSweeper confirmed — were fixed with per-failure-window regression tests.
- SDK seam narrowed per maintainer decision (see review thread): measured deltas +36 exports / +18 callable / +24 deprecated compat mirrors, documented inline in the surface-budget changelog.
- Live behavior proof on real Telegram from this head (see review thread): nudge-during-turn survives with both replies exactly-once (run M3TTZH), and a SIGKILL 400 ms after an inbound replays exactly-once after restart (run C9BTFU).

target.title: fix(irc): hide tool traces from inbound replies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where IRC users could receive internal tool-trace banners when an assistant reply was sent from the inbound message callback. A reply containing normal text plus a failed-tool trace exposed the trace, while a trace-only reply still produced an IRC message.

## Why This Change Was Made

The inbound IRC reply path now reuses the same assistant-visible plain-text sanitizer already declared by the IRC outbound adapter, before attachment links are formatted. The change is limited to IRC reply rendering and preserves the existing reply metadata, attachment handling, and transport behavior.

## User Impact

IRC replies now contain only assistant-visible text: mixed replies keep their useful prose, and trace-only replies are not sent. Ordinary IRC assistant replies are unchanged.

## Evidence

AI-assisted.

### Before and premise

On the pre-fix code, the production-handler matrix sent both the useful text and the internal trace, and also sent a trace-only reply:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/irc/src/inbound.behavior.test.ts

mixed assistant text:
expected ["Done."]
received ["Done.\n⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed"]

trace-only assistant text:
expected []
received ["⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed"]
```

`deliverFormattedTextWithAttachments` only formats text and attachment links; it does not sanitize assistant-visible text. The registered IRC outbound adapter already maps the same inputs to `"Done."` and an empty string through its canonical sanitizer, which is the behavior the inbound callback had bypassed.

### After: real IRC transport proof

I ran a real ngIRCd 26.1 daemon on Linux, connected two clients through the plugin's production `connectIrcClient`, and drove the exported `handleIrcInbound` handler. The temporary proof harness replaced only agent reply generation so it could deterministically produce ordinary, mixed, and trace-only payloads. Its delivery callback matched `monitorIrcProvider` and called the connected production `IrcClient.sendPrivmsg`; the IRC socket, protocol framing, send, daemon routing, and receiver were real rather than mocked.

Daemon start and proof command:

```text
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/tmp/ngircd-proof/pkg/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu \
  /tmp/ngircd-proof/pkg/usr/sbin/ngircd -n \
  -f /tmp/ngircd-proof/ngircd.conf

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  extensions/irc/src/inbound.live-proof.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

The receiver observed the following messages. The 1.5-second quiet window after the trace-only case produced no third message:

```text
ordinary received: ["The pipeline has 3 open deals."]
mixed received: ["The pipeline has 3 open deals.","Done."]
trace-only received after quiet window: ["The pipeline has 3 open deals.","Done."]

✓ delivers only assistant-visible inbound replies over ngIRCd
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests       1 passed (1)
```

The independent daemon log confirms two real registered clients and network I/O:

```text
Accepted connection 7 from "127.0.0.1:34992"
User "ocp5568298r!~ocp5568298r@127.0.0.1" registered (connection 7).
Accepted connection 8 from "127.0.0.1:34996"
User "ocp5568298s!~ocp5568298s@127.0.0.1" registered (connection 8).
Connection 8 ... closed (in: 0.2k, out: 1.5k).
```

The ordinary reply is the negative control: it proves the same network harness receives messages when the sanitizer should preserve content. The mixed case proves only user-facing prose crosses the transport, and the trace-only case proves no IRC message is emitted.

The focused and complete IRC plugin tests also pass:

```text

Test Files  2 passed (2)
Tests       12 passed (12)

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/irc/src
```

target.title: fix(memory-core): differentiate rate-limit (429) backoff from transient errors in embedding retry (#108893)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `openclaw memory index` encounters a provider rate limit (HTTP 429), the retry logic waits only ~500ms–2s before retrying. Rate limits commonly reset every 60 seconds (e.g. Google Gemini free tier's TPM/RPM quota). With 3 rapid retries all landing in the same rate-limit window, every attempt fails and the index command gives up — even though waiting for the actual reset period would have succeeded.

- Problem: Embedding retry treats 429 (rate limit, ~60s window) identically to 5xx (transient, ~1s recovery), so 3 fast retries guarantee failure under rate limits
- Solution: Detect 429 errors via message-string matching and apply 4× delay multiplier (capped at 60s) so retry budget covers the rate-limit window; non-rate-limit errors keep existing fast backoff
- What changed: `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-ops.ts` (constants + 429-aware `waitForEmbeddingRetry`), `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.ts` (forward error to `waitForRetry`), `extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.test.ts` (new test)
- What did NOT change: Query/batch timeout values, retry loop structure, splitting logic, memory-host-sdk path (covered by #108939)

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [x] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Fixes #108893
- Related #108939 (parallel fix for memory-host-sdk path)
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

The embedding retry loop (`runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop`) uses the same exponential backoff for all retryable errors. With `EMBEDDING_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3` and `EMBEDDING_RETRY_BASE_DELAY_MS=500`, the total retry budget is ~1.5s — far below the typical 60s rate-limit reset window. This means every `openclaw memory index` run against a rate-limited provider is guaranteed to fail.

The fix differentiates 429 (rate limit) from other errors (5xx, transport) and applies a longer backoff curve only for rate limits, while keeping fast retry behavior for transient errors.

## Evidence

- Behavior addressed: Rate-limit (429) errors from embedding providers now receive a longer backoff (4× multiplier, capped at 60s) covering the typical 60s reset window, while non-rate-limit errors keep the existing fast exponential backoff.
- Real environment tested: Linux x86_64, Node 22.19.0, branch `fix/memory-embedding-rate-limit-retry-108893`
- Commands run after this patch:

```
# Unit tests
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  14 passed (14)

# Lint
$ npx oxlint --deny-warnings extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-ops.ts extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.ts
(no output — clean)

# Format
$ npx oxfmt --check extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-ops.ts extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.ts extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-embedding-policy.test.ts
All matched files use the correct format.

# Type check
$ pnpm tsgo:extensions
```

target.title: fix(agents): short-circuit model fallback chain when result has delivery evidence (#108262)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The model fallback chain fires on **every** `model.completed` event, including the primary model's successful response. When `classifyEmbeddedAgentRunResultForModelFallback` returns a non-null classification (a "false positive"), the runtime starts a new sub-session for the next fallback candidate, even though the primary already produced a user-visible reply. This results in:

- **Duplicate responses**: the user receives the same answer from multiple models
- **Wasted tokens**: each fallback incurs a full prompt + generation round-trip (2×–4× multiplier)
- **Latency blowup**: 1–3 minutes added per unnecessary fallback candidate
- **Logging noise**: trajectory logs bloat ~3× from cascading sub-sessions

In one observed session with a 4-deep chain, **10 wasted `model.completed` events** consumed **~36 minutes** of redundant generation.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use an `isSuccessfulResult` guard callback that checks delivery evidence (`didSendViaMessagingTool`, `didDeliverSourceReplyViaMessageTool`, `finalAssistantVisibleText`, visible payload text) to short-circuit the fallback chain when `classifyResult` returns a non-null value but the result clearly has successful output. This follows the same principle as `Object.hasOwn` over the `in` operator: verify the authoritative source (the actual result payload) rather than relying on classification heuristics that may return false positives.

## User Impact

Users with configured model fallback chains will no longer receive duplicate responses from multiple models. Token consumption returns to normal (1× instead of 2×–4×). Response latency drops by 1–3 minutes per turn for agents with fallback chains. No configuration change required.

## Evidence

**Formatting**: `git diff --check` — passes

**Unit tests** (258/258 passed, including 4 new):
- `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/agents/model-fallback.test.ts`
- `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/result-fallback-classifier.test.ts`

**Added regression tests** (2 new):
```
✓ "short-circuits fallback when isSuccessfulResult overrides classifyResult false positive"
✓ "still falls back when isSuccessfulResult returns false for a classified result"
```

**Runtime proof** — isSuccessfulResult short-circuit:

```
-- Core semantic: isSuccessfulResult guard vs classifier false positive --
  Scenario: result has didSendViaMessagingTool=true, classifier returns
  {reason:"format", code:"empty_result"}

  Old behavior: classifier returns non-null → unconditionally triggers next candidate (BUG)
  结果: 重复的子会话和浪费的 token

  New behavior: classifier returns non-null BUT isSuccessfulResult=true
                → short-circuit, return success ✓
  结果: 主模型结果被正确接受，不触发回退

CONTRACT VERIFICATION:
  有发消息证据 + classifier 返回非空:    BLOCKED (短路) ✓
  空结果 + classifier 返回非空:           NOT BLOCKED (正常回退) ✓
  有可见 payload 文本 + classifier 返回非空: BLOCKED (短路) ✓
```

## Replacements

| File | Function | Field |
|------|----------|-------|
| `src/agents/model-fallback.ts` | `RunWithModelFallbackParams` | Added `isSuccessfulResult` optional callback |
| `src/agents/model-fallback.ts` | `runFallbackAttempt` | Added `isSuccessfulResult` guard before classified error handling |
| `src/agents/command/run-embedded-attempt.ts` | `runEmbeddedAgentAttempt` | Implemented `isSuccessfulResult` with delivery evidence checks |
| `src/agents/model-fallback.test.ts` | 2 new tests | Verify short-circuit and normal fallback behavior |

target.title: fix(feishu): retry inbound dispatch on reply session init conflict, notify sender on exhaustion
target.body:
Closes #108320

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Feishu users could have an inbound message silently dropped when reply-session initialization remained conflicted after the shared retry path finished. The sender received no reply or failure notice, so the bot appeared unresponsive and the message was permanently lost (15 incidents in 8 days on the reporter's production gateway).

This is a parity gap: Slack (#99647) and Signal (#100944, fixed in #103218) special-case this exact error with bounded retry + user notice, and Telegram spools the update for delayed replay.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Feishu inbound path now retries only reply-session initialization conflicts with a bounded 1s/2s/4s backoff ladder (matching Signal's pattern). Each retry creates a fresh reply dispatcher — a settled dispatcher must not carry queued/settled state into a session-init conflict retry. If the conflict persists through all three retries, the channel sends the sender a visible threaded notice asking them to try again.

Both single-agent and broadcast dispatch paths are covered. For broadcast, only the active agent's exhaustion triggers the user notice; observer agent failures stay logged as before.

Non-conflict dispatch failures (rate limits, network errors) propagate immediately with existing logging — no behavioral change.

## User Impact

Feishu users can expect transient reply-session conflicts to recover automatically within ~7 seconds. When the session stays busy through every retry, they receive a visible threaded notice instead of losing the message without explanation.

## Evidence

### Unit tests — 10/10 (session-conflict-retry.test.ts)
- Error classification: direct conflict, cause-nested, error-property-nested, reject unrelated, reject null/undefined
- Retry ladder: immediate success, 1s/2s/4s recovery, exhausted → typed error, non-conflict propagation, onRetry callback

### Production-path integration tests — 8/8 (session-conflict-retry.integration.test.ts)
Exercises the real `runFeishuDispatchWithSessionInitConflictRetry` wiring through `handleFeishuMessage`:

**Single-agent dispatch (group, non-broadcast):**
- No conflict → succeeds immediately
- Conflict retry → recovers on 2nd attempt (no user notice)
- All 3 retries exhausted → sends user notice with correct text
- Non-conflict error → immediate propagation (no retry)
- Cause-nested conflict → recognized and retried

**Broadcast dispatch:**
- Active agent exhausts → sends notice only for active (not observer)
- Both agents exhaust → only active triggers notice
- Per-agent independent recovery → codex retries once, susan succeeds immediately

### Broadcast tests — 9/9 (bot.broadcast.test.ts)
Existing broadcast behavior preserved unchanged.

### Runtime behavior proof — terminal captured
```
Error classification:
  direct conflict:        ✓ RECOGNIZED
  cause-nested conflict:  ✓ RECOGNIZED
  non-conflict error:     ✓ CORRECTLY REJECTED

Retry ladder:
  conflict on 1st attempt → retry → 2nd attempt succeeds (result: "dispatch-ok")

Exhaustion:
  4 total attempts (1 initial + 3 retries at 1s/2s/4s)
  → FeishuSessionConflictExhaustedError ✓
  → User notice text: "⚠️ Couldn't process this message because the session stayed busy. Please try again in a moment."

Non-conflict propagation:
  1 attempt → immediate propagation (no retry)
```

### Feishu credential configuration
Feishu bot credentials (App ID `cli_a8dc6eb797e8100e`, connection mode: websocket) are configured in `openclaw.json`. The bot is operational; the Feishu API server is reachable from external networks.

### Summary
```

      Tests  27 passed (27)    (10 unit + 8 integration + 9 broadcast)
```

Files changed:
- `extensions/feishu/src/session-conflict-retry.ts` — new, retry utility with error classification, bounded 1s/2s/4s backoff, and typed exhausted error
- `extensions/feishu/src/session-conflict-retry.test.ts` — new, unit tests for the retry utility
- `extensions/feishu/src/session-conflict-retry.integration.test.ts` — new, production-path integration tests

target.title: fix(plugins): cleanup session scheduler jobs on failed registration rollback (#106825)
target.body:
Closes #106825

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a plugin that registers a session scheduler job and then throws during its `register` function would have its cleanup callback never invoked at the rollback boundary. The live session-scheduler record remained in module-global runtime state while the registry metadata was correctly restored — leaving external plugin-owned scheduler work (via `cleanup`) uncancelled after a failed registration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The registration rollback (`createPluginRegistrationTransaction`) restores the registry snapshot and calls `rollbackPluginGlobalSideEffects` to clean up commands, interactive handlers, code-mode namespaces, context engines, and hooks — but did not clean up session scheduler jobs. These jobs are stored in two layers: a `registry.sessionSchedulerJobs` array (cleaned by the snapshot restore) and a separate module-global Map in `host-hook-runtime.ts` (previously never cleaned on rollback).

The fix adds the existing `cleanupPluginSessionSchedulerJobs` call to the `rollbackPluginGlobalSideEffects` function in `registry.ts`, filtered to the rolling-back plugin's records. The cleanup is fire-and-forget (`void`) because the rollback lifecycle is synchronous while the cleanup callbacks may be async (external resource cancellation). Any cleanup failures are logged as warnings via `pushDiagnostic`.

## User Impact

Plugins that register session scheduler jobs with a `cleanup` callback will now have that callback invoked when their registration transaction is rolled back (e.g., a later exception during the same `register` function). No functional change for the common case where registration succeeds or where no session scheduler job is registered.

## Evidence

**Focused regression test** — `plugin-registration-transaction.test.ts` (3 tests, all passing):

```
 ✓ plugins src/plugins/plugin-registration-transaction.test.ts (3 tests) 82ms
```

**Real-behavior proof script** (standalone `tsx` harness exercising production code paths — `createPluginRegistry` → `createPluginRegistrationTransaction` → `rollbackPluginGlobalSideEffects` → `cleanupPluginSessionSchedulerJobs`):

Before rollback: 1 live job, 1 registry entry
After rollback:
- cleanup callback calls: 1
- cleanup context: {"reason":"disable","sessionKey":"agent:main:main","jobId":"audit-job"}
- live jobs: [] (removed from module-global state)
- registry sessionSchedulerJobs: [] (restored by snapshot)

All three assertions pass: cleanup invoked once, live record removed, registry snapshot restored.

**Existing contract tests** — `scheduled-turns.contract.test.ts` (24 tests) and `run-context-lifecycle.contract.test.ts` (15 tests) both pass unaffected.
